short: The FAA roadmap for assuring the safety of AI in aircraft. Its distinction between static and adapting models, and its account of what AI breaks in certification.
title: The FAA Roadmap for AI Safety Assurance
subtitle: Learned AI, learning AI, and the assurance chain that AI breaks
body_html:
On this page

  • The sentence worth reading twice
  • Learned AI and learning AI
  • The six principles
  • The safety continuum
  • The milestones, and where they stand
  • The part that has dated
  • Why this matters outside aviation
  • Primary sources

The one-paragraph answer

The FAA Roadmap for Artificial Intelligence Safety Assurance, Version I, signed July 23, 2024, is the FAA’s first formal statement of how it intends to assure the safety of AI in aircraft. It sets six guiding principles, separates learned AI that is static in operation from learning AI that keeps adapting, and says plainly that AI breaks the requirements traceability on which certification has always depended. It is explicitly a living document. No successor version has been published as of this page’s date.

The sentence worth reading twice

Most AI governance documents describe what should be done. This one describes what stops working, and it does so in a single paragraph that is worth quoting because a paraphrase weakens it:

“When AI is used to develop a learned AI implementation, those links are broken; the designer cannot derive the requirements that directly describe the AI implementation and cannot validate them by showing that they provide coverage to the next higher level.”

FAA, Roadmap for Artificial Intelligence Safety Assurance, Version I (2024)

The links in question are the spine of safety engineering. Aircraft requirements produce system requirements, which produce item requirements, which produce a design that can be verified back up the chain. Every step is justified by rational explanation and traceability.

The roadmap points out that in a learned system the lowest-level requirement is the model. As it puts it, this may be a large neural network with thousands of weights performing basic arithmetic that cannot be traced to higher level requirements. There is nothing to explain in the way the process expects, because nobody wrote it.

That is not a documentation gap. It is the reason AI assurance needs new methods rather than better paperwork, and it is the clearest statement of the problem published by any US regulator.

Learned AI and learning AI

The roadmap’s most portable idea is a two-way split, and it is careful to say the terms are its own because the field has no agreed ones.

  • Learned AI is static in the operating environment. Trained offline, assured at design time, then fixed. A designer may gather in-service data, retrain, and deploy a new version, but each new version is subjected to safety assurance.
  • Learning AI is dynamic in the operating environment. The learning mechanism is inside the deployed system, and the roadmap states the consequence directly: it is not possible to qualify each version, so the assurance strategy has to address the learning itself.

The roadmap declines to pretend the second is solved. It says learning systems pose safety concerns if assurance is not properly addressed, treats them as an ongoing research topic, and notes they may adapt in a way that degrades performance and weakens their original safety profile. It raises recurrent certification as a possibility rather than a plan.

For learned AI it names the tension that any regulated deployment will recognise: in-service data makes it possible to spot deficiencies quickly, but the frequency of updating is constrained by the need to assure each update. Assurance is the brake on the improvement loop. The roadmap asks for methods that are sufficient and proportional to a revision rather than treating every retrain as a new aircraft.

The six principles

  • Work within the aviation ecosystem. Use existing safety requirements rather than building a parallel regime for AI.
  • Focus on safety assurance and safety enhancements. Both the safety of AI and the use of AI for safety.
  • Avoid personification. Treat AI as a tool, not a human, and avoid human-centric language so responsibility stays clearly assigned.
  • Differentiate between learned and learning AI.
  • Take an incremental approach. The roadmap argues that a single guideline defining the evidence needed for all AI applications may not be feasible, usable or appropriate.
  • Leverage the safety continuum.

A seventh, leveraging industry consensus standards, sits alongside them. Avoid personification is the one to notice. It is a governance principle disguised as a style rule: calling a system a copilot or an assistant quietly reassigns responsibility, and in a regime where the designer is answerable for the design, that matters.

The roadmap also draws a boundary. The treatment of the ethical use of AI is expressly outside its scope.

The safety continuum

The continuum is the FAA’s existing idea that the level of safety society expects varies with the operation: highest for scheduled passenger service, lower for experimental flight and small uncrewed aircraft. The roadmap uses it as a sequencing device, gaining experience where the consequence of being wrong is smallest, then carrying the methods upward.

This is risk tiering by consequence, the same instinct as high-impact AI in OMB M-25-21 and the risk tiers of the EU AI Act, but grounded in a regime that has been calibrating it for decades rather than inventing it for AI.

The roadmap also notes that machine learning is already in production safety systems: the Aircraft Collision Avoidance System standard replaced the scenario-based design of TCAS with weighted risk models developed through machine learning in ACAS X.

The milestones, and where they stand

Version I published a timeline. These are its dated commitments, with what can and cannot be confirmed from public sources.

MilestoneScheduledStatus
Policy statement: introduction of AI in aircraft certification, directing applicants to disclose AI use and discuss a certification path early4Q2024 draftNot publicly confirmed
Policy memo: considerations for AI/ML in airborne systems and equipment4Q2024 draftNot publicly confirmed
Training-based methods research; data analytics research4Q2024Not publicly confirmed
Introduction to AI Safety Assurance training for FAA and designee workforce3Q2025Not publicly confirmed
Research: aberrant behavior, systems and testing strategy, risk modeling, software runtime assurance4Q2025Not publicly confirmed
Certification Position Papers documenting stable policy for specific AI/ML use cases1Q2026Not publicly confirmed
Research: numerical methods2Q2026Not publicly confirmed
Advisory Circulars; industry standards via SAE G34 and EUROCAETBDNo date given

Not publicly confirmed does not mean not delivered. Policy memos, issue papers and certification position papers are working instruments between the FAA and an applicant, and several are not routinely published. The honest statement is that a reader outside the process cannot verify them from open sources, which is itself worth knowing before relying on a date.

What can be said: as of this page, the FAA’s AI/ML discipline page still points to Version I, and no Version II has been published. For a document the FAA describes as a point-in-time snapshot of a fast-paced technology, that is the fact to watch.

The part that has dated

The roadmap places itself inside Executive Order 14110 on the safe, secure and trustworthy development of AI, issued in October 2023, and devotes a section to that national context.

EO 14110 was revoked in January 2025 and replaced by Executive Order 14179, which is the order every federal AI document written since then cites, from OMB M-25-21 to the Department of War AI strategy. So the roadmap’s national framing rests on an order that no longer exists.

Separate the two layers before concluding anything from that. The policy framing has been superseded. The engineering reasoning has not: requirements traceability breaks for learned systems whichever executive order is in force, and no change of administration alters that. This is the same discipline these pages apply to agency enforcement posture, which moves, against statutes, which do not.

Why this matters outside aviation

Three things here generalise, and nothing about them is specific to aircraft.

The learned and learning distinction is the right first question for any regulated AI deployment. A static model can be assured once and re-assured on each version. A model that adapts in place cannot be, and needs assurance built into the operating environment instead. Most organisations have not asked which kind they are running.

Assurance is the constraint on the retraining loop. Aviation states it explicitly; medical devices, credit models and hiring tools face the same arithmetic without always naming it. If every retrain requires re-assurance, the cost of assurance sets the update frequency, which sets how quickly a model can be corrected.

Traceability is where AI actually breaks the existing regime. Any compliance regime that asks why a system produced a result, and there are many, is asking for a link the model does not have. The FAA said so first and said it plainly.

Primary sources

  • FAA, Roadmap for Artificial Intelligence Safety Assurance, Version I, 31 pages, signed July 23, 2024 by David H. Boulter, Associate Administrator for Aviation Safety. faa.gov
  • FAA, Roadmap to AI/ML at the FAA, briefing to the REDAC Subcommittee on Aircraft Safety by Dr Trung T. Pham, March 2023. The work plan that preceded Version I, prompted by a subcommittee finding that industry was reluctant to adopt AI/ML because of certification uncertainty.
  • ARP4754A and ARP4761, cited in the roadmap for the system safety methodology behind design assurance levels; DO-178C for software development.
  • Executive Order 14110, October 30, 2023, cited by the roadmap and since revoked.
